title: How Curious Are You Really
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece distinguishes two forms of curiosity that leaders often conflate: task curiosity, a detective-like focus on understanding a specific problem or opportunity, and intellectual curiosity, an open-ended pursuit of new ideas unconnected to any current assignment. It argues most leaders possess healthy task curiosity, which supports focused learning and strategy, but genuinely intellectually curious leaders are rarer, even though that trait is what fuels lifelong learning and breakthrough thinking. The author notes a modern obstacle: search-engine algorithms tend to narrow exposure to new subjects rather than expand it, making intellectual curiosity harder to cultivate than in the past despite unprecedented information access. It closes by urging leaders to deliberately read widely across formats and subjects to counteract this narrowing effect.
points: Task curiosity (solving a specific problem) and intellectual curiosity (open-ended exploration) are distinct, and most leaders only have the former.
Intellectual curiosity's payoff is unclear by design, the learning itself is the reward, which makes it harder to prioritize than task-driven inquiry.
Modern search-engine algorithms tend to narrow information exposure rather than expand it, making genuine intellectual curiosity harder to sustain today.
Deliberately reading widely across formats and subjects is offered as the practical antidote to algorithmically narrowed curiosity.
quotes: Task curiosity describes the interest leaders and practitioners take when confronting a problem or opportunity.
But it is not the kind of curiosity that shapes lifelong learning and that leads to big insights and breakthrough thinking.
Intellectual curiosity is about constantly looking for new information and seeking novel ways to combine this data with what one already knows.
Unfortunately, the algorithms used by contemporary search engines tend to narrow our exposure to new subjects rather than expand them.
Nothing stimulates intellectual curiosity like reading widely in different formats and media on a variety of subjects, topics, and issues.
